utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. May I remind the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the usher to give the witness a set of the statement and documents that we will be using during the cross-examination so that he can refer to the documents as needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, you can just leave the documents there; you don't need to look at them now. When we come to a document, then I will ask you to look at it. Yesterday in answer to my questions you said that at one point after the liberation of Vukovar General Colonel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: -- came from Miladinovac to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It was in the month of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw the warning. It's Lieutenant General Vladimir Stojanovic who came with a delegation from Miladinovac to the Vukovar area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have document 0D00-0321 on the screen? This is the B/C/S version. The English is 0D00-0323. For everyone's information, this is document number 2 in the set that we have provided, so you can follow that more easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you see this document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we please zoom in a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This is an order from the command of the 1st Military District, strictly confidential 234-2, dated the 19th of November, 1991. And it's stated in the document that the command of the 1st Military District forbids the exchange of SFRY OS prisoners for the prisoners of the armed formations of the Republic of Croatia without the permission of the below-signed Chief of Staff of the 1st Military District. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you know about this while you were on the territory of Vukovar or during the briefings that you had?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document into evidence, if there are no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit Number 442.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you were describing your assignments relating to the evacuation and security of the members of the so-called Mitnica group at Ovcara. You said that according to you that was on the 19th of November, 1991, at 10.00, the reference is the transcript 16 -- page 16 of the unofficial transcript, line 19. You also said that you thought that the same day they came to Ovcara and they were evacuated that same day. That is in the transcript on page 17, line 8. Could you please tell me if you don't remember dates well or events?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the events better than I remember the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that the Mitnica group was brought to the Ovcara sector on the 18th of November, 1991, would you be able to confirm, perhaps, that because so much time has passed, almost 15 years since then, you don't remember all the details as well as you did before?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. A person cannot remember everything that happened at the time. It was 15 years ago. All I know is that we properly received, guarded, and handed over the Mitnica group.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In response to a question by my learned friend you also said that these prisoners from Mitnica were taken over by you after they were disembarked into the Ovcara hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after they were brought to the Ovcara hangar, and that is when we took over the security.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in the statement that you provided to the OTP investigators you said that Vezmarovic organised the evacuation of these people to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was responsible for the transport and their evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Captain Vezmarovic, with his military policemen, came to the Ovcara region before the prisoners of war from Mitnica were brought there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that this is what he stated before this Trial Chamber, would you agree with that or would you allow for the possibility that you do not recall all the details relating to the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall all the details. I don't know that he was there at that time. All I know is that afterwards he had the assignment of transporting them in an organised manner to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you allow for the possibility that he was there and that he was waiting for the convoy of the prisoners of war from Mitnica at the Ovcara farm on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point, I cannot really remember whether he waited for the convoy or not. I mean, if he said that, what can I say?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at Exhibit 432 on the monitors now? This is the notebook of Captain Vezmarovic, and if we can please look at page 63.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect to my learned friend, this is Vezmarovic's document. This witness, as far as I am aware, has no -- has played no part in its compilation. How can a witness answer questions in relation to a document which he does not compile and the groundwork has not even been laid whether he knows what the content might be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am not going to ask the witness about the authenticity of the document. All I wanted to do was to show him an entry which relates to one of my previous questions and maybe that would refresh his recollection, because he said that he didn't recall all the events all that well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it still has the problem posed by Mr. Moore, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that there is no problem. It's an entry dealing with the war prisoners from Mitnica, when they were received, who they were handed over to, when they were transported. So I would just like to know if the witness recalls all these details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I provided an explanation to this question. I don't have any other explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would suggest, Mr. Vasic, that's about as far as you can take it, isn't it? The witness says he simply doesn't remember. Mr. Moore objects to you putting to him other people's documents, about which this man says he has no recollection and no knowledge, to remind him. You can remind him by his own documents and his own unit's documents. Is there something more?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness said that Mr. Vezmarovic, I assume in compliance with his order, was involved in the evacuation and transport of these prisoners of war to Sremska Mitrovica. This entry that I am talking about was something that was on the basis of an order of the 80th Brigade, and the company commander was Mr. Vezmarovic. I don't need to read the document, perhaps, and I can ask the witness if he recalls that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of November --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember that on the 18th of November, around 1600 hours, at the Ovcara farm the military police of your unit took over control of the prisoners of war from Mitnica?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say what time it was. All I know is that on the night of the 18th and the 19th we were guarding prisoners of war at Ovcara until they were evacuated and handed over at Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 19th of November, 1991, at about 1130 hours, Captain Vezmarovic handed over the prisoners to Captain Karanfilov?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Captain Vezmarovic took the list of prisoners to the Mitrovica KP Dom on the 19th of November, 1991, at 1530 hours and gave them to Lieutenant-Colonel Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the military police company of the 80th Motorised Brigade was not involved in securing these POWs on their way from Ovcara to Sremska Mitrovica and that Captain Vezmarovic was the only one who left with those lists, and this actually occurred after the convoy had already left Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I thought that Vezmarovic was there all along, that he went with all the other soldiers, that he took the lists with him, and that was all I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you did not see the members of the military police company of the 80th Brigade on the 19th of November in the morning hours or after 1200 hours at the command post of the 80th Brigade in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were always some policemen there at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you know anything to suggest that the military police company of the 80th Motorised Brigade, once these prisoners had been handed over to Captain Karanfilov, returned to its headquarters in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not get the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is Mitnica -- or rather, from Mitrovica, when the prisoners were handed over, they returned to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember at what time the military police company of the 80th Brigade returned on the 19th of November, 1991, as you claim, from Sremska Mitrovica to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I think it was the fall of darkness already.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What if I tell you that Mr. Vezmarovic, when facing this honourable Chamber, said that he carried the lists to Mitrovica himself following the convoy, trying to catch up with the convoy, that his military policemen were not involved in the evacuation there? Would you agree with that, sir? Would that jog your memory to any extent?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I can't say exactly. Since Vezmarovic was going, I'm sure he wasn't going on his own. He must have taken some police officers with him or soldiers, but I'm not sure how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that much is certain. Captain Vezmarovic had to enjoy some degree of safety on his way. He was the commander of the military police company. But tell me, how many policemen would that have required, for example, such a task as to secure the Mitnica group convoy?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A platoon. Detachment to platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to this. I don't want to interrupt my learned friend, but the witness has repeatedly said that he doesn't know, I can't say, I can't say exactly. And then he's being asked to guess about what would be required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it's more than a guess, Mr. Moore. This is the commander of the unit in which Captain Vezmarovic served. I would allow the question, but I do point out, Mr. Vasic, that I'm not quite sure what significance you think we can attach to this. You have the evidence of Captain Vezmarovic. You have this witness with a different or incomplete recollection of the events. You have identified that this witness has a different recollection, and he says he, apart from a few basic things, he don't know the details anymore. Captain Vezmarovic gave you detailed evidence about these matters. You are not going to strengthen the evidence of Vezmarovic by pursuing questions like this with the witness who doesn't remember. Unless you have some other purpose, could I just point that out to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your guidance, Your Honour. We have a witness here testifying about things that happened 15 years ago, and that's precisely what I want to know: How vivid are his memories in relation to what happened on the 19th and 20th of November in Vukovar. He happened to be the commander of a unit which was part of these events, and that was what this particular set of questions was based on: The evacuation and the events before the 20th of November. This is something that the subject of the indictment. That was the end of my set of questions in relation to Mr. Vezmarovic. Now I'd like to ask the witness something else. He should know who these POWs at the Ovcara farm had been taken over from.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who brought them to Ovcara before the military police company and the command officers of your brigade took over?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they had been brought by the security organ of Operations Group South. They were brought there, we took charge, and we provided security until their eventual hand-over.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember telling Captain Vezmarovic when they were brought on the 18th of November, 1991, to -- from then on take orders from Captain Karanfilov as far as anything to do with the POWs was concerned?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember Karanfilov [Realtime transcript read in error missing word "Karanfilov"] or those events. I know there was a group of people from Mitnica there. I know Vezmarovic was there, but my officers were there, too. However, I don't remember any details. In actual fact, I don't really think that matters. The important thing is they were secured, they were escorted, and they were finally handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the set of statements, your own statements, in front of you. There was the statement you gave to the investigating judge of the special department of the Novi Sad court on the 21st of November, 2003. Page 3 -- page 6 in B/C/S, and the page in English is 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that's happening, Mr. Vasic, could I just point out line 20. I think in the first sentence the answer was, "I don't know remember Karanfilov or those events." The name was missed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. The witness said he did not remember Karanfilov in those events, Captain Karanfilov in those events. What I wanted to do was jog his memory about his 2003 statement. Maybe his memory was more vivid at the time than it is today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you have that, sir, page 6 in the B/C/S version of your statement to the investigating magistrate? The thicker set with your statements.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The statement you gave to the investigating magistrate, Alimpic, from the special department of the basic court. Have you got that, sir? The statement is dated the 21st of November, 2003?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please turn -- first of all, did you, in fact, provide this statement to the investigating magistrate, and you still remember that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please go to page 6 in the B/C/S of the that statement. If you could please look at paragraph 2, there's just one sentence. It reads: "It's possible that I gave Captain Vezmarovic -- that he was there to receive orders from Captain or Major Karanfilov." Did you state this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about after this, do you perhaps now remember seeing Captain Karanfilov at Ovcara on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't actually remember seeing him from where I stand now. I tried to picture the way he would have looked. Hair greying; perhaps slightly smaller, shorter, that is, than I am; not of such strong build. We didn't talk that much, actually, he and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What about your chief of security, Dragi Vukosavljevic, did he perhaps tell you that Captain Karanfilov was perhaps a member of some counter-intelligence group, something to do with Sid, a group operating in the area of Ovcara, Jakubovac, and Grabovo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those counter-intelligence organs are always a bit secretive, they always have their own principles of work. They report to their own commanders to the extent that they believe is necessary. I heard about this group - what exactly did you say? - counter-intelligence, yes, right, in Vukovar, but I don't know that Karanfilov was part of that group. I believed at the time and I still believe that Karanfilov was actually part of the operations group, that he was a member of the operations group.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified in chief yesterday about your own involvement with securing the transport of civilians, those who spent the night at Ovcara between the 19th and the 20th of November, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know, perhaps, that this convoy was supposed to be taken to Croatian territory near the village of Lipovac along the Zagreb-Belgrade highway on the 19th of November, 1991, but the simple fact of the matter was the Croatians refused to have it back and that was why it had to be returned to the Vukovar area, sent back to the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time. I did hear later on about that, and I saw this for myself. I got on to one of the buses and I greeted the people there. I told them not to worry, that everything would eventually be fine, and asked them where it was that they wanted to go. I thought they should go to Sremska Mitrovica, but a group of people said they wanted to go back to Croatia. I told them that at this point in time it was impossible to cross over into Croatia for security reasons, which they accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Nonetheless, the convoy left for Nustar that morning - do you know about this? - but the Croatian forces wouldn't have them and they had to be sent back yet again?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Even this early they demanded to go back to Nustar, but they weren't let through, at least that's what I heard at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At long last the convoy was forced to return to Croatia across Sremska Mitrovica and Bosnia, the long way around. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who from your unit was providing security for this convoy of civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure that (redacted) was there and a group of other officers, but I can't remember their names one by one. I spent the entire night with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it wasn't deliberate, but I think there will have to be a redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Redaction in the answer commencing at 23 on our screen. I mention "our" screen, because it's evident that different circuits produce different line numbers in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who handed out the assignment to secure this group and who was it you reported to once the operation had been completed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who handed out the assignment, and according to our military rules, Colonel Mrksic was the only person for me to report to at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the military police company and your brigade's chief of security were part of this convoy's security?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they should have been. I know that there were soldiers, military policemen, I'm not sure how many. I know that (redacted) was there with his own group of soldiers, and we spent the entire night there, because I toured the unit, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, unfortunately my question was very specific and the answer was pretty broad.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't tell you one by one, I can't give you everybody's names.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, this is about one particular name that seems to be at stake here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I know it is a lot to ask you, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: (redacted); and therefore, we have to delete it, if it's mentioned in this courtroom, from the transcript. It would be a help if you could avoid mentioning that name. Now, I know that you're having to think about questions and try and remember events a long time ago, and it may be asking too much of you to try and remember not to use that name. But if you could be aware of the problem and, if possible, not actually mention that name. You could mention, perhaps, just say, "a particular captain."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand, Your Honour. I'm not trying to deliberately avoid names. The simple truth of the matter is: I didn't know people that well. I met most of those people for the first time on the 7th. I got to know them to some extent. He was an officer at the command, and I knew him to some extent. But I still don't really know most of those people; they were reservists, that was another reason. That's why I'm saying this. I can only use him as a point of reference for other kinds of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What if I tell you that the chief of security of your brigade and the police chief says that they were not informed about this evacuation of civilians, that they were not involved, can you confirm that? Can you explain how it can possibly happen that the chief of security and the commander of the military police are not informed about an assignment like this? How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that they were not informed, but what is certain is that some soldiers from their units were there. I don't know if any of these two gentlemen were actually present, but I know that I was there with some soldiers from their units and the captain we referred to a while ago, as well as some of their officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who was in charge of security assessments as far as the civilians at Ovcara on the 19th were concerned?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there was any detailed security assessment being made. People arrived in buses; guards were set up all around the place, officers and soldiers, to protect those people. And the regime remained in force until their departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who was in control of the security regime, the escort for the civilian convoy that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember who exactly that was. I was there myself as well. So if I was there, I was probably the most senior officer around. I don't know if there was anyone more senior than me there, either in terms of position or in terms of rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I understand you were there and you were handling the security. Could you please tell us who took over the convoy on the 20th of November from you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. A group of people came, I don't know who they were, where they were from. They introduced themselves, they had vehicles, they had escorted the convoy where they thought it should go, where they intended it to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were these people that you are talking about, were they in uniforms? Were they civilians? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time it was hard to establish whether somebody was a civilian or not. Everybody was wearing half uniforms, half civilian clothes, so I can't remember. I don't recall asking them who they were. We probably talked, and that's how we handed these people over.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm asking you. Do you know to whom you handed over the people who were then transported further?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't recall right now to whom I handed them over. Somebody who came with that assignment, with some sort of authorisation, somebody who introduced themselves as having come with that particular assignment. We checked it properly, they were allowed to take the convoy, there were no problems, you know, regarding this hand-over.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What you're saying now, is that something that you recall, or are you assuming that that's how it was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it should have been. Nobody could have come and taken the convoy and just have left. I mean, we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you also provide logistics for the convoy that spent the night at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So there was a request for logistics supply for the convoy?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in some conversation we came to the conclusion that we needed to protect the women and children. In the immediate vicinity there was an agricultural combine, a cattle farm. They had cows, other livestock, and we went there. I think the name of the director was Markovic or Petrovic, and we asked him to help us, to give warm milk to the children, so we gave them what he gave us. In the morning, before they left, we again offered them tea and milk.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: During the convoy's stay, did you make a list of the persons there, and then did you hand these persons over using the lists to the people who came to take over the convoy?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall anyone making a list of the persons. I don't remember handing them over. In reference to the list I think that there were eight or nine buses, and in the same way that they arrived in the buses, they were driven away.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember when the convoy arrived at the Ovcara farm on the 19th of November, whether your units were already there in the hangar, and did they wait for the convoy or were they engaged later?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we came later to the buses and took over guarding them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand, you only got to the buses only when you found out that they had arrived?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who brought them to us. I mean, the buses couldn't have come by themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, all I was asking is whether you came with your units to the Ovcara farm once you found out that they were in your sector, that they had arrived in your sector?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No units were there, other than those of this captain that we talked about. He was there with a group of soldiers and his officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And he informed you that the convoy had arrived at Ovcara and that it needed to be guarded?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really say who informed me, but I believe that we needed to guard it. Someone must have told me that that is what we needed to do, so that is what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we move to private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please zoom in on the right portion of the map? The right part. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, please, with the usher's assistance, take the magic pen - as my learned friend Mr. Moore likes to call it - and use it to mark a few things on the map. With the number 1 could you please mark the local command of Ovcara; and with the number 2, the local command Jakubovac and Grabovo; with the number 3, the command post of Sotin, if there was such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the Sotin command was in the centre, in the very centre of town. There was a school there. As for Jakubovac and Grabovo, I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could go further down. No, we should scroll up, and then we may be able to see Grabovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Am I mistaken in believing that Grabovo must be somewhere close to the photograph, under Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grabovo should be around there somewhere. As for the Ovcara command post, it was somewhere along the road from Sotin, next to this house here.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the house there was the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Next to where it says "Ovcara," could you place a number 1 there. That was the command post of Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And circle that as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Before my learned friend proceeds, if he looks at map 5 of the bundle, that may assist him in some way because it mentions Grabovo on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe my learned friend is right. I would like to thank him for his assistance. But as regards the layout, I believe this map is a better one and the scale is more favourable as well. Perhaps we can mark this map and then we can move on to the other one suggested by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please use the number 2 to mark the command post of Jakubovac? Do you see where Jakubovac is?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We can't see Grabovo, it is just underneath the photograph, but could you use the number 3 to mark the Sotin command place?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Command post. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since the witness confirmed that Grabovo is underneath the photograph, would it suffice for the Chamber if the witness puts the number 4 right next to the photograph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, as it's not shown, it's better not to be marked. I think we know where it is by now; it's on more than one other exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your instruction. I agree fully. I would like to tender this photograph, and we will not be using it anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 443.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, at the beginning of this cross and today, you reiterated that the tactical group of the 195th Motorised Brigade commanded by Lieutenant-Colonel Milan Jovic stayed within your establishment for a relatively short time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What was the exact period, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not part of our establishment for more than three or four days at the most. Because we didn't issue a single task to them, they came there to the sector. He reported to me, he asked to be deployed to be given time to rest, and to go through their equipment and materiel. They did so, and after that they were no longer part of the establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd of November, 1991, do you remember issuing an order, strictly confidential number 34-2, changing the command post for Grabovo, Jakubovac, and Ovcara, and you appointed the commander of the tactical group of the 195th Motorised Brigade, Lieutenant-Colonel Jovic, appointing him the local commander of the places, effectively declaring the previous orders null and void?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat this last answer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did appoint him, but I did not know that he would soon, one or two days later, no longer be part of our establishment. I thought he would be staying with us for some time, and that was the reason I appointed him to that particular position.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And that was why you gave him a specific assignment, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm for me that under the rules governing the garrison and barracks service, a local commander must establish and preserve order and discipline, ensure the safety of persons and property, make sure any prisons and detention units function properly, and there is always the obligation for unit commanders who happen to be in the area covered by a local command to be familiarised with the rules of behavior in such an area, those imposed by the local commander. Do you know about these rules?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's perfectly in keeping with all the regulations that I know about, that I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that your unit or, rather, you as the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, was -- were appointed the local commander in Jakubovac, Ovcara, and Grabovo on the 18th of November, 1991, by a decision of OG South, and that was after the departure of the 20th Partisan Brigade, which was the unit from which you took over your assignment?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me if you asked your brigade's chief of security to make a security assessment covering the new area of responsibility and to define the possible axis from which your unit might be attacked, having deployed your men on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's always a security assessment that is drawn up in relation to all units. I'm certain that at one point and in some way one was made I don't know when exactly or what it said, but each unit had its own axes within its area. Maybe, once the fighting was over, everybody was beginning to relax a little because people believed that there would no longer be any danger to our commands or our manpower, so people felt more comfortable and were more relaxed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, in this area and in keeping with your command's order, did you organise, set-up, proper authorities under the rules of service in the armed forces and under the rules governing the work of garrisons and life in barracks? Did you take all the security measures that were necessary?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't quite apply the garrison and barracks rules to this, because those were peacetime rules, rules of service and all sets of rules familiar to me. These were extraordinary conditions. This was just after combat, just after the fighting had ended, but all the steps were taken to ensure the safety of our units, of the civilians, and of the entire environment. This applied to all the units in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you took all the appropriate steps to protect the citizens, the population, from mistreatment, from people entering their houses without proper authorisation and searching them, and this was in keeping with the order that at that time prevailed throughout the territory which you had previously taken, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you draft instructions for their work in order to ensure that the population could get on with their lives?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if there was an order or a set of instructions that was drafted and applied to all, or if that was just something that was done based on some sort of a standard form and then was merely adapted to our own conditions on the ground as we went along.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have Exhibit 418 shown? Thank you. For the benefit of my learned friends, this is 0467-2869; that is the ERN number. Thank you. Can we please have page 2 of this document shown? It's a report. And can we please try to zoom in on the upper half of the page. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, you see this. This is the report indicating that you took over the area of responsibility from Lieutenant-Colonel Misovic from the 20th Partisan Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If you could please look at paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We no longer have this on our screens. If could you please zoom in on the upper half of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Item 4, the last bullet says, "In the course of the day the tactical group of the 195 Motorised Brigade entered the composition of OG South. It was 450 men strong and was resubordinated to the 80th Motorised Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which date was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The report is dated the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was resubordinated; I'm not sure about its numerical strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This is a regular combat report?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm not saying anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have just finished a set of questions, and this might be a convenient time to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have a break. A half hour is required because of the redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Before the break we spoke about the local commands. It is my belief that you used the written and oral orders that we mentioned to divide your area of responsibility up into the local commands, belonging to your subordinate officers; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You answered one of my questions about the liberation of Vukovar, about the 18th of November, 1991. Do you know that on this occasion, the Yugoslav flag, the three-coloured flag, was hoisted on the so-called water-tower in Vukovar, that this was done to mark the liberation of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how you found about this, that Vukovar was liberated and who from, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I heard this at the command of OG South. I believe -- or rather, I am sure that the three-coloured flag was hoisted to the top of the water-tower by the Chief of Staff, Miodrag Panic. Some officers came who were stationed across the Vuka River, they came to the Negoslavci area. So several different people told me. There were several sources, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you said that you had not been informed about the hospital evacuation, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You were not informed about the fact that the POWs from the hospital would be taken to Ovcara, that is, to your area of responsibility, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Exhibit 375 displayed now? The 19th of November at 1800 hours, that is the entry that I'm interested in. For the benefit of my learned friends, this is page 10 of the English. If we could please just zoom in slightly on this particular entry. That is the last page of the log, the date is the 19th of November, 1800 hours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, what you can see in front of you is the war log of the 80th Motorised Brigade, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: There is this entry for the 19th of November 1800 hours, and it says: "The Ustashas were captured in the morning hours and were taken to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica. There was combat in the hospital area only, where the remaining ZNG and MUP members are expected to surrender (about 200). An order came to be at the ready in order to organise a security regime or the guarding of prisoners." Do you see that entry, the 19th of November, 1800 hours?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who you got this from, who told you about this, to get ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting my learned friend. The translation we have, we don't have any reference to an order. Clearly that's important. I wonder, perhaps, if the witness could be shown the actual handwritten document, and he can then confirm whether that is there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is no problem at all. If I could have the usher's assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, can you see that on your screen; is that a clear image for you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking about the 19th of November, 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That's what I'm talking about. Does it say precisely as I read out?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. I can say for sure that I was not aware of this. The war log is kept by an officer. It is with a very high degree of certainty, and with full responsibility, that I can tell you I knew nothing about this, although this entry was made to my war log. I don't know how this came about or who heard about this, whether this was done by some other people, the entries there. So I have nothing to add in that respect. But one thing I do have to repeat is we were not involved in any sort of security regime for the POWs from the hospital. I didn't even know that they were there. I, as the commander, didn't know until the moment they were brought to the area surrounding the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who could possibly have been familiar with these entries to the war diary, I'm talking about the people from your command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's usually one person who is put in charge of this, working under the supervision of the Chief of Staff of the commander. These are serious issues being discussed. The security organ might have known about this, perhaps somebody else, but one thing that can be said is not everybody had access to the war log. I can see that this was being kept by Jankovic, Major Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Major Jankovic was the person keeping this log. But someone had to tell Major Jankovic about this for him to record this in the war log, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, someone certainly told him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You did say that the Chief of Staff was responsible for any entries made to the war log. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was his responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When an entry like this is made to the war log, certain steps should be taken in order to get ready for this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Nonetheless, you say you were not informed about this, so probably if I ask you if anyone from the command, the chief of security or the military police commander were familiar with this, you would probably say no; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the security organ, the security officer; he might have been informed. I don't believe the military police company commander was, though. One thing that is remarkable is that nobody informed me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On the ground in Vukovar, back in 1991, was there any other command body or command structure in place that was outside of the regular command structure? Was there anyone who could have led to something like this being entered into the war log without the commander's knowledge, unbeknownst to the commander?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no other structure, no other body. This is quite obviously a document from my brigade, no one else could have made the entry, save for Major Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know if on the evening of the 19th or the morning of the 20th any preparations were, in fact, carried out in order to set up a security regime for this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. What about your earlier statements, both to the OTP and in Belgrade, did you ever say that during the hospital evacuation on the 20th of November, 1991, a platoon of the traffic police belonging to your brigade was used to escort the convoy on its way from the hospital to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. I did give a number of statements. I thought -- or I believed that one of the traffic officers were there, but not the traffic police. I later found out that none of the traffic officers were involved either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is my understanding correct of what you just said about the traffic people being involved in 2003 and 2004 - that's when you said it - but you checked later on and now you believe that they were not involved?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do believe that they were not involved, although did I say that there were a couple of traffic people there. But I have since received new information to show that they had, in fact, never been involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you clarify for us how you got this information after 2004, how did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same as you did. I listened to reports from people, I followed the testimonies in Novi Sad, in Belgrade. I think that the Novi Sad Dnevnik newspaper wrote about that most extensively. I don't think that any of the officers said that the traffic police were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to talk with any of the traffic police people who were in that platoon at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- perhaps I did, but I don't know that they were in the -- in the traffic platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, then, on -- how did you conclude earlier that this unit was involved in the evacuation of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit, well, I saw it when it came to the hangar. I saw Vukasinovic and he said to me that these were soldiers from the hospital, the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I asked you about the members of your own traffic police. How did you earlier, when you gave the statements, conclude that they took part in the evacuation? What were your sources for making this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the sources exactly. It was probably based on conversations with officers in the brigade after the fact. When we were discussing the situation, what happened, how did it happen, probably somebody told me then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who was the platoon commander of the traffic platoon in the military police company of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: During the evacuation of the hospital, did you discuss the use of this platoon with Mr. Vezmarovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this is not a company. These are two traffic detachments or two traffic squads. I don't remember discussing that with Vezmarovic, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about Dragi Vukosavljevic, your chief of security?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said before that I didn't really feel comfortable saying something that I didn't remember. I don't recall speaking with Dragi. Why would I talk to him when it was all over anyway? I was busy with other duties in town, and when it was all over, when it was passed, I wasn't really interested anymore in who was where.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I asked you this because earlier you mentioned that you talked to some people from your unit who participated, so I thought perhaps it was Dragi Vukosavljevic amongst those people?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know. Perhaps I did. I mean, I did speak with some other people. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If this platoon or these two squads of traffic police were used during the evacuation of the hospital, who would have to be informed about that in your command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the company commander, the security organ, the chief of the transport section.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that you maybe talked about [as interpreted] the chief of the transport sector about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really remember. No, I was thinking about major who was in Sotin, but he wasn't chief of the transport unit, he was a commander of a battalion, but I can't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me, would I be making a mistake if I were to say that in all of your statements you said that you noticed the prisoners of war at Ovcara for the first time on the 20th at around 1700 hours?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are holding me to certain times and dates. I note -- I remember certain events. When I saw the prisoners, I think it was sometime before it got dark, at dusk. I don't really know what time it was. I wasn't really thinking about seeing what time it was. There were things that I had to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that we have a report here by the hydrometeorological institute establishing that at that time it was getting dark at approximately 1700 hours, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. I was coming back from Sotin. I didn't stay there for very long, and when I got there, yeah, that would be that, it was getting dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer cautiously my next question so that we don't have to go into private session. And my question is: Didn't the local commander of Ovcara before you arrived, which you just talked about, if -- you came to the hangar, didn't he inform you that some soldiers and other people were coming to his area of responsibility and was it his duty to inform you about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really remember, again, whether he informed me or not. I know that I was with him there. He informed me, as the superior commander, according to the establishment, but at the time he really wasn't under my command, even though we were there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you informed, before you came at dusk, about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I wasn't informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In any case, you're sure that you saw the buses at dusk?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was passing through that sector with -- where (redacted) command was in the afternoon when I was going to Sotin. I didn't see anything then. I don't know whether, after I went to Sotin in the meantime something happened. All I know is that when I came back, I saw buses. (redacted) came out to greet me as the -- me being the commander, so I didn’t stop where he was. I continued in front of the hangar to see who it was, what is going on, and I explained all of these actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I did ask you to be cautious about the names.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say that you stayed about 30 minutes at Ovcara and that after that you were rushing to get to the regular briefing at the operations command.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there about 30 minutes for sure - it could be five minutes more or less - but that's how long I was there. It was time; I was supposed to go to the briefing, to the local command post in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In view of that, that would mean that you came to the OG command in Negoslavci a little bit before 1800 hours when it was almost over?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was between 16 and 1800 hours. I was late. I explained already yesterday what the situation was, and I think that there is no need for me to go into that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Of course. Would I be correct if I said that for some reason you are not giving us the correct time-line when you went to Ovcara on the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry? Again, when I what?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you went to Ovcara on the 20th of November, you are not giving us the correct time for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not giving you the correct time? I didn't look at my watch to see what time it was, but I went there to see what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I think that you came to Ovcara much earlier than you say here. You said that this was at dusk, and a witness here said that he saw you at around 1400 hours and that you were in front of the hangar at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What could have happened was that I could have just passed by the hangar, according to what I remember, and then continued on to Sotin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The witness said that at the time you were trying to protect the prisoners from the gauntlet, at that time, and that he saw Lieutenant-Colonel Panic there also at that point.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was protecting the prisoners right from the moment when I saw them, and I protected them with that man and his group of soldiers until the time that they entered the hangar. We did everything to prevent the abuse and harassment when they were going through the gauntlet. I didn't see Panic. Later I read Panic's statement and that he saw me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you kindly tell us where you read this statement by Lieutenant-Colonel Miodrag Panic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in some newspaper reporting on the testimony; that's where I read it. And secondly, Panic himself told me when we met at the military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at Exhibit 371, please? This is the operations diary of the 80th Motorised Brigade. If we can look at the entry of the 20th of November at 1600 hours, and that would be on page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, we will have this on the screen shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in on the lower part of the page, because that's the last entry on this page of the operations diary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, can you see the entry starting at 1600 hours?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And does it state there that: "The brigade commander requests that shifts of officers be assigned" --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: -- "for guarding the captured ZNG and MUP members. The military police company and brigade command officers were engaged for this."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what date? This is for the 20th?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the 20th of November at 1600 hours, and we can check that if we scroll the page down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You see this entry, that's what it says?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like not to comment on this, but I would like to explain. I did say that I wasn't stating the correct times because I cannot remember everything. This was written arbitrarily by the person who was recording entries, but that's not how it was. I was asking for assistance in officers and soldiers to be sent to protect the prisoners who came from the hospital to the hangar. This was written down, but it doesn't have to be correct, and for sure it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: First of all, are you claiming that the war documents of your units are incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what's in question. It's one entry that we are dealing with here. The objective was the protection of the civilians, of the people. It was formulated properly, this entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you kindly tell me if the Chief of Staff of the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade is the one who controls all the entries in the war operations diary of that unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what he should do, and he should control that, but this doesn't happen always. This is usually done by one person. An operations officer is given the assignment of recording all the events. But this was just an arbitrarily-written entry, but it's quite clear what this is about. I sought assistance; I asked for officers and soldiers to come to help with the protection of the prisoners as they were entering the hangar. And of course it was logical to have this assistance from officers and soldiers from a command that was nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So could you please tell us whether this person in your command who maintains the war documents, does he write down what he is told?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He writes down things in the way he understands them. He's not a fully-trained person. He is not told exactly what to say; he is not given the specifics. He is just simply told: Such and such a thing is happening. This is going on at Ovcara, so the commander is asking for shifts of officers. So why would we need officers there, in view of the assignment that we had?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We're going to do this later.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not properly formulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What I would like to ask you is whether this person who was not fully trained happened to be the director of an enterprise in Kragujevac?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But he was just superficially trained for military duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I am going to ask you whether your Chief of Staff, Lieutenant-Colonel Danilovic, controlled these entries, these documents?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes, he was supposed to do that, but he wasn't checking up every single thing. In principle, this is just a duty given to somebody to carry out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you just assert that the person who was the local commander was threatened at his command post at 1600 hours in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for sure he was. A larger, armed group of people appeared in his immediate vicinity, he don't know who they were, where they were from, what they were doing there. They were all carrying weapons; they were being quite aggressive, arrogant. He didn't know who their officers were; he was only there with two or three soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All right. We know how many soldiers he had; I'm not going to ask you about that. But what I will ask you is if you are of the opinion that a unit like this could use anti-aircraft guns in order to protect itself, 20-millimetre guns in order -- against live strength?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could it use an anti-aircraft gun in order to protect itself against men? They only had semi-automatic weapons. And how could they use these weapons against a group of people they didn't know and they were not under attack? A person would undertake measures in order to protect themselves and was requesting protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So in your words, there was no threat at this time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was worried about the safety of his command and his men. He is not necessarily under threat, but he did think about taking steps to protect himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At this point in time is there a military police company of the 80th Motorised Brigade inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where it was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably on their way -- on their way back from Sremska Mitrovica, on the road back to Negoslavci, or even in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On their way back from Sremska Mitrovica. You're not saying that the military police company from Sremska Mitrovica is taking a whole day to reach Negoslavci, are you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They handed over the prisoners, the Mitnica group. Of course it might take a whole day, unless it was done in a timely manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What if the group surrendered on the 19th of November at 1530 hours? This military police company of the 80th Brigade, weren't they supposed to long have been in Negoslavci on the 19th of November, by 1600 hours?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's an open question. Should they have been there? Shouldn't they have been there? Were they facing problems back there or not? That's a different cup of tea.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You, as brigade commander, did you know where your military police company was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of November at 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see that -- I did see some of the soldiers, but I didn't see the entire unit. I didn't see Vezmarovic or anybody. I know that some of them did go to Sremska Mitrovica, and I did see some of them later at Ovcara. There were certain indicators at the time that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I am afraid I will have to clarify this. You knew that they were, in fact, in Negoslavci, or did you believe that they were on their way back from Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How, then, did you request that a unit be used of whose whereabouts you knew nothing?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When did I make that request?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Operations log, 20th of November, 1600 hours. You requested that the military police company be used, and the brigade command officers, for security, as this reads, or for protection, as you say. One thing that is beyond doubt is that you requested that the military police company be used. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that the phrasing of this entry at 1600 hours is just not accurate. Maybe the officer who was keeping the log didn't do it properly. I requested assistance from officers and soldiers in order to help the prisoners without knowing where the military police company was or the rest of it. I did not request the assistance of any other officers. I requested that one or two officers be sent over with a group of soldiers to protect the prisoners. I didn't know about the military police company; I didn't know that it was there. I believed them to be somewhere on their way back from Mitrovica to Negoslavci. Where they were at this precise point in time is not something I knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, could I point out that at least in the English version there are two sentences in the entry. The first records, or purports to, the commander's request; the second seems to indicate what was done about the request, rather than it being the request of the commander that the military police and others be assigned to the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't believe this is quite what it states in our language. In the first portion there is the security assignment, you are quite right there. As for the other portion, it reads: "Responsibility for this," so somebody is announced as the person, "to carry out this assignment, the military police company and the brigade officer." That's the first part of the sentence, and in the second part of the sentence you have: "The implementing agency," as it were, who is supposed to carry this out. That's the second part of this sentence, and this is one sentence comprising two different parts containing these two different bits of information, or at least that is my reading of what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I just point out that, at least as it's rendered in English, it's simply two statements. The first is a request, the second is what was done about it. If it's something different in your language, that translation needs to be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'm looking at the English, and the translation comprises two sentences; the B/C/S contains only one sentence. There is a comma.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As I understood you, it's still, even as you translated it, wasn't saying that the brigade commander had requested the military police and brigade command officers to undertake the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, right at the beginning of this sentence it says that the brigade commander was the one who requested this. In column number 4, which is right next to this entry, side by side, it says Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, as far as I understand, he was the person who ordered this entry be made. And we can check with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not order this entry to be made. It was the person who was in charge of making the entries, and he wrote down that I was requesting assistance. The wording of this report is erroneous. I didn't know about the military police company, I didn't even know its whereabouts, as you have suggested. I was asking for officers -- I was asking for two officers, I know that for sure, and a group of soldiers to be assigned to us; the reason being, Vezmarovic was not there. And because of this, Captain Vukic came with a group of soldiers from the staff command, from the signals company, and the rest of them. And I sent him, as I said yesterday, to go and speak to Major Vukasinovic, in case there was an assignment or in case any assistance was needed. Vukasinovic turned him down, turned him away, by saying that there was an assignment for him and told him that he should go back to Negoslavci, which is what Vukic did, in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us then: How did you forward this request to your brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, as I have already said. I'm not sure if I phoned them; I'm not sure if somebody actually went there. We did say that someone from his command called and reported this. I don't know how it happened, but the duty operations officer at the brigade command eventually received this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If this was done by phone, where from? Do you know that? Which phone did you use?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it was from one of the brigade's cars. Some of them had phones, actually. Not all of them by any means, but some did. I'm not committing myself on this one, however. I did phone them from somewhere or other.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Which specific units did you contact by using this telephone that you have now mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less all of them, the subordinate commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that Mr. Vezmarovic told us that his military police unit was at Ovcara, even in his absence, and that he himself only arrived later, what can you tell me about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that there were soldiers wearing white belts there and other soldiers, too, from the staff command, the signalsmen, and so on and so forth. I'm not saying that there was nobody else there; there were soldiers wearing white belts, even in my vehicle. I'm not sure if anyone else was there, but ultimately there were other soldiers there wearing white belts. I have no idea who they were. I told you, I came to this unit very late in the day, and this was the first time I met those people. Despite my best intentions, I had no time to meet them all individually, not even their officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What was the assignment of this unit that you requested to be sent to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To help Major Vukasinovic out protecting the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You were an officer of a higher rank than Major Vukasinovic. Did you appeal to you for help?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Why did you then order a unit to come over from Negoslavci, from the brigade command, to go over there and help you out?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I had not seen Vukasinovic there in the hangar up to this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If you had not yet seen Vukasinovic in the hangar, how then could you possibly have asked for assistance on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was requesting assistance in order to protect the command post for my own protection, for the protection of prisoners. It was only once I had entered the hangar that I realised Vukasinovic was there, and help had not yet arrived by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you were requesting assistance before you entered the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
