utterances.text: Yes, and as soon as I realised what the situation was outside the hangar, all the things being done, this man came with me, with his own group of soldiers and officers, and we started getting some work done. And we stayed right there until all the prisoners were inside the hangar. It was only this point in time that I entered. This went on for 25 or 30 minutes, and then I went inside and I was surprised to see Vukasinovic right there in the middle. In the meantime, Captain Vukic had arrived, and I told him to go and speak to Vukasinovic, to ask him about help or about any assignments. He went and spoke to him. He said there were no assignments, so he came back and he said: Are we at ease? And he said: Yes, you are at ease. After Negoslavci -- he gathered his soldiers and they all drove back to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about this group of soldiers from your command? Why did you not send them to help the local commander, but rather Major Vukasinovic instead?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Major Vukasinovic was the most senior officer there and he was from our superior command. Also, he was in charge of the prisoners because he was the one who had brought them there to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ask Major Vukasinovic if he needed any assistance?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because help had already arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who was in the command of the unit that had just arrived?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reserve Captain Vukic. I can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you there when the unit came?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was still there, and I was the one who warned him about everything and I was the one who told him to go and speak to Vukasinovic. It was at this point in time that I left for the command post to see Captain [as interpreted] Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you in command of the unit inside the hangar since you were the highest-ranking officer there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I left immediately, having spoken to this officer, having told him to go and address Vukasinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you not supposed to act differently, given what the situation was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did everything that any professional soldier would have been able to do in a situation like that. A group of armed people emerged; we had no idea who they were or where they had come from. Their intentions were not clear. Their assignments were unknown. I took steps to protect myself, my subordinate command, and the prisoners. I think any military officer would have done the same, facing the odds that I was facing. Regardless of the fact that I didn't know for sure who it was that was inside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Based on what you're telling me now, it looks to me as if you had asked for this unit to come over and help you and the local commander and not Major Vukasinovic - wait a minute, please, let me finish my question - to protect you, to protect the local command, and the prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You were the highest ranking officer there. Why didn't you take charge in the hangar, why didn't you take over the command of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no idea who those people were. I was the highest ranking officer, in terms of rank; that's true. But there was an officer there from my superior command, a security officer. I'm not sure why you are refusing to see this, to understand what I'm saying. He was the one who had brought those people there. That was his assignment, he had gone to get them and he brought them over. He was given this assignment by his own superior officer, not by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, you say you reckoned at the time that your safety was under threat as well as the safety of the command post within your area of responsibility, your area of command. We've covered that. You, being the local commander of the area, Ovcara, Grabovo, Jakubovac, you were supposed to take charge, to take over the -- to take over command, and you were supposed to protect all these elements who, in your opinion, had come under threat; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that people were under threat, were in peril, the prisoners, my command, myself, in no particular order. We were all in peril: The prisoners, myself, my command staff. Those prisoners had been brought there by Major Vukasinovic, an officer from my superior command. I don't know where he had brought them from or what the assignment had been. How can I possibly order him about if I had no idea what these prisoners were there for or what was supposed to be done with them?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ask him who these people were, these units, who they had surrendered to and where they had come from?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did ask who the prisoners were. I saw people there wearing different kinds of clothes, some people were wearing white overcoats, some were wearing combined uniforms, some were wearing caps. That was the first time I laid eyes on those people, so I asked Vukasinovic: Vukasinovic, who are these people? Where did you get them from? And he said: These are people from the hospital, they are prisoners. That was all he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So it's not quite true that you don't know who the people were and where they had been brought from?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was once I was inside the hangar that he told me these people were from the hospital. I hadn't realised up until that point; I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You, as the local commander there, did you have the powers to take any steps that you were entitled to take under the law and as the local commander?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no authority to take his prisoners away because this man was carrying out an order previously given by a superior command. I just reported to my superior commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When did you report to your immediate [as interpreted] commander? You say immediately, what exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the prisoners were inside the hangar, when I had done my best to protect them to the extent that I could, when help had arrived from the brigade command, led by Vukic. When I went inside the hangar, when I realised Vukasinovic was there, he told me who these people were. And then there was group of soldiers that was brought over, between 15 and 20 of them. I thought to myself: Here was a man from my superior command. I supposed that he had been given an assignment, I offered him my help, and he refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander he reported to immediately, Major Vukasinovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That evening after Vukic had arrived, I told Vukic to go and speak to Vukasinovic; that was the assignment I gave him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it is time for our midday break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. I left you running because I realised you were at a point of some interest. We will adjourn now and resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.33 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Judge Parker is unable to sit this afternoon, so Judge Thelin and I will sit, according to the Rules. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, before the break we were discussing the units which arrived when you asked for them to go to the hangar at Ovcara. You told us that you didn't know where the military police company of the 80th Brigade was at the time and that the entry in the war diary pertaining to the 20th of November at 1400 hours is an erroneous one?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is imprecise, incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that the aforementioned local commander in his testimony on page 7707, line 11, stated that you were there with two officers, two military policemen in the vehicle, that you came from Sotin, and that you invited the military police to come from Negoslavci to secure the prisoners, would you say that he was wrong as well?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked for assistance, and it is correct that I was with another two policemen in the vehicle. Vukic was there and not Vezmarovic, and I issued the assignment to Vukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What I put to you contains two important factors. One is the use of the military police, as you yourself mentioned, and that you told that to Lukic [as interpreted] and that Vezmarovic was not there. The second being was that the purpose of the unit was to secure the prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which unit exactly? The one led by Captain Vukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The unit you summoned, and by what you said, they were brought there by Captain Vukic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were there to protect the command, myself, and the hangar, and the prisoners when entering the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I understood properly, the unit arrived after the prisoners had entered the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that precisely, but the entry into the hangar was coming to a close.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you on that occasion ask for any other of your resubordinated units, or did you only ask for the command of the 80th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the command of the brigade only.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us why Captain Vezmarovic didn't come. Wasn't that the task to be executed by the commander of the military police and the military police in general?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume Vezmarovic at that time wasn't there, and I decided to call Vukic; that was the decision I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Where was Captain Vezmarovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Somewhere on the road between Mitrovica and Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that Captain Vezmarovic, on the 19th of November, 1991, was in Sremska Mitrovica rather than on the 20th of November when these events were taking place, could we conclude then that your statement is illogical?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prisoners were taken away on the 20th in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me which prisoners were taken away on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Mitnica unit, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit 371 put on the screen? Could we please have the entry pertaining to the 19th of November at noon. For my learned friend from the OTP, that is page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, could you see the entry pertaining to the 19th of November at 12.00?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't read it quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let me do it for you. "We were informed that a decision has been issued that captured members of the ZNG be transferred to Sremska Mitrovica. Lieutenant-Colonel Danilovic relieved of responsibility concerning the guarding of captured MUP and ZNG members in the Ovcara sector." Is this entry correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 19th, pertaining to the Mitnica group, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This is the entry for 12.00 on the 19th concerning the prisoners who were at that moment in the Ovcara sector, obviously secured by your unit, as stated in your operations diary.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the hospital prisoners were there on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, the hospital prisoners were there on the 20th, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Rade Danilovic was there - this regards the Mitnica group - he was there with them, and this is what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you see the date and the time when this group was transferred to Sremska Mitrovica? The entry is for the 19th of November at noon.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to be transferred to Sremska Mitrovica. Is that what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is this entry correct, and does it tally with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that the Mitnica unit prisoners were transferred, handed over; I don't know the details. The time seems to be all right. I don't know whether this entry is formulated in the proper way, but I know that they were transferred and handed over on time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And the commander of the military police company, Captain Vezmarovic, left together with them in the morning to deliver the list in Sremska Mitrovica; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who went there to give the list, but in any case it was in existence and it was taken there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now you are stating that you don't know who compiled the list and who delivered?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I know it was compiled, it was typed, I saw it, and it was then taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Where did you see it being typed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it on my table at the command concerning the Mitnica group members. Number 1 was their commander, Filip Karaula, and then all the subsequent people in numbers up to the number 90 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when is it that you saw this list on your desk at the command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What date?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe when they had left on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know who forwarded the list to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be certain. I could guess, but the list was put together in any case. I saw it and, out of curiosity, I went down the list to see the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was tasked with compiling the list?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You stated that the unit of your military police escorted the convoy up to Sremska Mitrovica, handed over the prisoners to someone. And now you're telling us who was tasked with compiling the list or who delivered it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It wasn't important to me who made the list. It was important that it was made and delivered, the same way the prisoners were handed over, and that there were no incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who was responsible to you as the brigade commander for the list and the handing over of the prisoners from Mitnica?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Your chief of security, Dragi Vukosavljevic, was he present when the Mitnica group departed on the 19th of November, around noon, as stated in the operations diary?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. He probably was engaged in some part of that operation, but as to whether he was there when they departed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Captain Vezmarovic couldn't have been in Sremska Mitrovica on the 20th, as you stated?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Then he must have been out in the field, implementing another assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As the commander and the duty officer of your unit, he never reported to you to -- that he was to go out in the field to complete a task?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to me. I don't know whether he spoke with the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you explain this then: In case of emergency how would your command be protected if you don't know where your military police commander is, and he was supposed to secure the command post?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It isn't only the military police that secures the command post, there were other units. There was a circular line of defence, and they all had their axes and the tasks and things to secure, as well as the military police. This all formed a single unit, a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Am I mistaken if I say that the military police were billeted close to where your command post was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you won't be. Perhaps two or three houses away from where we were. They were close, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did Captain Vezmarovic come by the command daily, several times a day, going to the house where he was billeted?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Vezmarovic had most contact with the security organ, and the tasks he was assigned were issued to him by the security organ or perhaps another officer. He didn't have much contact with me. I did see him occasionally, but I couldn't be there spending my time waiting for someone to come by. He was there, he worked well, and he was out in the field, there were communications, and he reported on the tasks. There was no need for me to be interested in that. As the brigade commander, I couldn't busy myself with every single unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Your Chief of Staff claimed that you were the only one to command the military police company?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction for the transcript, chief of security.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sometimes it can be so. But as to any routine or other task, the military police company never received it directly from me. Usually the tasks were issued via the security organ or perhaps by the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As regards this entry, pertaining to the 20th of November at 4.00 p.m., in which there is a request for some troops to come to Ovcara, does that refer to when you asked for some troops to come to assist? Can you explain why did you, as the local commander or the sector commander, ask for some troops to come? I believe you could only command and not ask.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed them, and I asked them to come, and me asking was something along the line of me issuing an order to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It seems to clear to me now, thank you. When you entered the hangar, did you see a rope there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There was a rope from the entrance to the hangar all the way until the far wall, and the prisoners were in that way more or less divided -- or rather, they were on one side and the TO members were on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you saw that rope, did you see members of your military police from your brigade in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw some people with white belts, but I don't know who they were, whether they were from that particular company.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As regards Captain Vezmarovic, was he there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I were told you that Captain Vezmarovic testified here that he put that rope up and that he placed the prisoners in one part of the hangar, does that mean that he must have been there where the rope was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That doesn't necessarily entail the presence of both, but if he said that he put it up, then it must be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that it wasn't possible for you to see the rope in the hangar without seeing Captain Vezmarovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree. There was commotion in the hangar; a large number of people were there in constant motion. I didn't move about the hangar much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In terms of his function, Captain Vezmarovic was supposed to command over the security detail there, because he was the commander of the military police company, and he must have approached you as the local commander and the brigade commander. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the most senior person there was Major Vukasinovic. If he was supposed to approach anyone, it was him. He knew he was the security organ, and it would be quite ordinary that he addressed him. I wasn't there, the local commander, and my unit wasn't there in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And isn't this facility in the Jakubovac-Grabovo-Ovcara sector?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And didn't we read an order here appointing you as the commander in this area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but I explained that my officer, the local commander of Ovcara, was not there at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you stand by your assertion that you did not see Captain Vezmarovic at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I don't remember seeing him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that you saw members of the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In front of and in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with my assertion that in your earlier testimonies you repeated several times that there was a total of 30 of them, both in front and inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That assertion is something that I cannot confirm or deny. Later, perhaps, I saw some more. I don't know if there were more of them, how many of them there were, whether there were 30 or 40. In any case, they were all armed with automatic weapons, some of them also had pistols and some other types of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said "armed with automatic weapons." You mean automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifles, different types of rifles. They didn't all have the same kind of rifle. There was also hunting weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would like to remind you about your earlier testimony as regarding the number of these troops. In your statement to the security organs on the 12th of January, 1998, and this is in the set that its first page is 0218-8336. And it's the page number L009-6424. Have you found it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't found it. I have the question -- I have the statement from Gojovic here in front of me. Is that the one you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, so that you don't trouble yourself, I'm going to give you my copy. The first page Mr. Vojnovic, do you see at the end of the second paragraph it says: "I recognised Stanko Vujanovic, Miroljub Vujovic, and a man there dressed by the name of Djekic."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And then you said: "As I recall, there were 20 to 30 of them in total."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that, but from what I recall there were more.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How many more?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How many more? Do you think it was up to 40?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. I cannot give you the exact number, but there were more. Now that I have that image before me, I think that there were more of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We're not going to be needing this statement any more. You told us that the local command and you personally were in danger, as well as the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Because of these 30 to 40 TO members; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: A unit numbering 15 to 20 people, a unit of the military police or any other unit, is that sufficient, together with the staff command unit that happened to be there, enough to confront this other unit that was there, numbering up to 40 people?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no intention of confronting them or entering into a conflict with them. We were there; we offered to provide protection. As far as the -- this aggressive stance of the TO members, I think it was better to avoid any confrontation. I think, as far as their behaviour was concerned, the behaviour of those TO members, that those soldiers would not have been able to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us today that Vukic came with 15 to 20 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Beside that, we heard from Captain Vezmarovic that they were members of a military police company. How many people of the 80th Brigade were there during the course of that day after you called them to the Ovcara farm?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right. You could say that there were about 40 people, including the police, if that's what Vezmarovic says, and those who came. But I would like you to keep in mind that Vukic's people returned to Negoslavci quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We must also add the soldiers who were under the command of the local commander to this number?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these were two or three soldiers; that was not a substantial force.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can I remind you that you, yourself, received three soldiers who help out in establishing order in the hangar and that the local commander had three more soldiers at least and there was certainly other soldiers guarding the local command post?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many there were with me, there were two for sure. I don't know how many the local commander had exactly. I mentioned we didn't go there to fight, I say that again. We came to protect those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ask the local commander for some soldiers from his unit at Ovcara that day to help you to establish order in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't have any soldiers. The soldiers that he had, if any, I think he did bring those soldiers, and they were there with us. And they were working to establish order and to provide some protection to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know the reserve officer named Jovan Novkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: He was the commander's deputy for morale, commander's assistant for morale?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did this officer lead a group of soldiers that was given to you to help to establish order in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Novkovic and the soldiers who were with him, I don't know how many there were. I know, and I said already, that there was a rope already put from one to the other end of Ovcara, and I also said and confirmed that I saw him. He was the assistant, as I said, of the said commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At the time did you see that any of the soldiers was making any kind of list of the prisoners of war in the hangar, or did this person himself do that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw a desk, and there was a person in uniform without a cap sitting at the desk. There were no ranks, no rank's insignia. I think that the person was a soldier or a conscript or a reservist. I don't know his name. He did start to make some sort of list. I didn't go up to him or ask him anything. All I saw was that he was sitting there, writing something down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you order for this list to be compiled?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was already under way when I entered the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know who ordered the list to be compiled?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I could perhaps make the assumption that it was the local commander who did that, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: From what you are telling me now, it transpires that the military police was there in the hangar before you entered the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. You see, there were soldiers going in to take a look out of curiosity, then they would come out, one soldier would go in and then perhaps come out again. But in this case that's not important. What's important is that somebody there began to write something, and I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I actually wanted to ask you the following: This person, this soldier, was not there out of curiosity; they were doing something there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, somebody must have told him. I don't know where they found the paper and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What would you say if I were to tell you that some witnesses assert that this list ended up on your desk, the desk that you mentioned at the brigade command, in the morning on the 21st of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would claim with certainty that that list never reached me. It's possible that it was mixed up together with the list of the Mitnica group, which was at -- on my desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that the commander, the local commander that we mentioned here before the Trial Chamber, said that he personally ordered that this list be placed on your desk, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say anything. I would say that I don't know anything about it. I know that the list of people from the Mitnica group was typed and placed on my desk. I read it from number 1 to number 90.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After the events at Ovcara, therefore after the 21st of November, 1991, did you ask the units or your brigade command to find and send this list to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because we were not in charge of those people, not dealing with their security. We didn't know how many of them came, how many were released; I read about it later. So I didn't have the intention or the desire to interfere in the work of the person who went and brought those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would be more likely to say that you knew how many there were, because it was the soldiers from your unit who were drafting the list?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody knew how many people there were, there was some guesses, some assumptions - they were incorrect - but it was in the range of 150 people or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss with the local commander - and you know who we're talking about - the list that you saw being drafted there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Because I also saw somewhere that he said that somewhere, and I gave the same answer that I am giving you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you assert that the list never reached the -- your command, but it ended up at the local command post?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not saying that it didn't reach the command, but it did not reach me or my desk. I assert that I did not see it. Maybe somebody placed it on the desk and then took it again. These are all possibilities and guesses, and that's something that is really not material here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, sir, you said that Captain Vukic came alone with soldiers to Ovcara, without other officers?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he came with Dacic -- actually, later I heard or read Vukic's statement. Dacic was there, Vukic was the commander though.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So the two of them were the only two officers who came with the soldiers. Were there no other officers at the command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were given the assignment from someone, and they were sent. From what I could see at the time, there was perhaps only Major Jankovic at the command out of all the active senior officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you were talking about the behaviour of the TO members towards the prisoners when you saw them in front of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that you intervened and you said -- described what was happening. Could you agree with me that they, the members of the TO, after your warning, did stop harassing the prisoners in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What does that mean, "not entirely"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were insults hurled, cursing, they were taken away from the ropes, there were threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But there was no physical abuse, if I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't think that there was any physical abuse later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: During the interview with OTP investigators, you said that you heard that Captain Vezmarovic established order in the hangar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For my learned friends, this is paragraph 35 of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When did you hear this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was after the rope was set up and after a certain time had passed, the time necessary to establish order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After the rope was placed and order was established, you left the hangar in the belief that everything would be all right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I was convinced, I saw that there was a sort of separation barrier put up. I don't want to keep mentioning him, but Major Vukasinovic stayed with them, with a group. I really can't say if they were officers or soldiers who were with him. In any event, they were not our soldiers from my group. So I felt sure that everything would proceed properly and that the same procedure would be repeated as with the Mitnica group.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Precisely the sort of situation that you have just described is the reason why you were able to rescue a married couple, two Croats, and to make it possible for that gentleman to go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember their names or if they were, in fact, married. There was a man who was sick, and there was a woman with him. And we sent them to our own medical station, which at the time was based in Sotin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And you left, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know those two were actually driven by us to the medical station. I realised that those two were exhausted or sick. I think I acted not only in a fair manner, but in a just manner, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After you left the hangar you went straight to the regular briefing at the OG South headquarters in Negoslavci, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You probably reached there before 1800 hours?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably between 1800 hours and 1900 hours, as I explained yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If we accept what you are saying and not what the operations log seems to be suggesting, that you were there at 1700 hours, namely that you spent 30 minutes there and not more, then you should have been in Negoslavci by 1800 hours, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was late to that meeting in Negoslavci; they started before I arrived. Don't hold me to the time or the place, but I was late to that meeting because of what had occurred at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The Defence wishes to put it to you that the briefings at Negoslavci always began at 1700 hours, because 1800 hours is the time for the combat report to be drafted. We say that you did come to the meeting, you were late at the meeting, you apologised, and you said there that you were personally involved in establishing order inside the hangar, but this was before 1800 hours, that's what we are saying.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to get all the dates and the time-line right. I know that it was night by the time I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you spent 30 minutes inside the hangar. You will probably agree with me when I say that it wouldn't have taken you half an hour to get from Ovcara to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree with that, but I may have passed by the brigade command on my way there to see if they were facing any difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If, in fact, you did go back to the brigade command, did you by any chance see Captain Vezmarovic there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He wasn't at the brigade command; he was two or three houses further down the street, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Why would you pass by the brigade command if you, in fact, had a radio link to them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To see if they knew anything about what else was going on, if they had information to share with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You were late to this meeting. Couldn't you have phoned them from the car?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I have? I was going straight there. This would have been quite difficult to explain over the phone since they were right there; it was easier to drop in on this them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you did say you were late to this meeting and it was a meeting at the superior command, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the reasons I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That was the reason you had run out of time to go to your own command, you were just wasting time there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said maybe I passed by the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, would it be logical for you to pass by your headquarters and waste more time, since you were late to this meeting already, as you were?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the situation was critical, it was a serious situation. I wanted to go straight there to see if there were any other orders or any information on what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say the situation was serious or critical and you were in a hurry to get to your superior command in order to see if there was anything new about the situation. What are you actually telling me?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what your understanding is of what I told you. If I went by the brigade command, if I passed by, I wanted to go by the operations room to see if there was any new information, any low-down on the situation and especially concerning the situation at Ovcara, if anybody had heard anything. But there was no new information on that particular development.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Wouldn't you expect to get new information at a briefing at your superior command? Wouldn't that be the first place you would go and look for information?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I might have phoned as well, might have asked about the commander's whereabouts. I still think it was justified for me to go to both places, Ovcara and the command, before I drove on to the command post. I still think I did the right thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who could possibly have phoned you asking for the commander?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, the commander of the operations group; he could have been on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And you were late to your meeting with that person, of all people, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This may be a personal thing for you or a logical thing if you like, but let's just move on. Is it true that you said that you only stayed at the meeting very briefly? This was a regular briefing at the OG command, and the meeting was nearing its end, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the meeting was drawing to a close. I'm not sure how much time was left exactly by the time I arrived. The meeting was drawing to a close. I came into the meeting and I apologised. I told the commander about the situation that I had encountered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I was just about to ask you how much time was left. Five minutes? 10 minutes? 15 minutes? 20 minutes? What do you mean when you say it was drawing to a close?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether it was five minutes or 20 minutes. It did go on for some time after I had arrived, that much is certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: For a short time though, you said?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a short time only.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At this point you walked into the operations room. You informed Mrksic about the problems at Ovcara, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say Mrksic was angry and he told you, "Don't even tell me about that."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "Don't even tell me about that."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Your report to Mrksic was in relation to the situation such that it was at the time you left the hangar at Ovcara, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just to make sure that I'm following, in answer to one of my questions you said the situation settled down, and that's what you told Mrksic, that there had been problems, that some prisoners had been beaten, but that when the units arrived the situation was sorted out, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not sorted out altogether, those people were still around, the TO people. They were still abusing people and making threats. Nobody knew exactly what they might be liable for, but they were at this point physically separated from the prisoners, the TO men. I did say that yesterday; I'm not sure why you keep returning to this. The security officer remained, the OG South security officer. He had an assignment - I'm not sure what the assignment was - and that for me, was a sufficient guarantee that the situation would remain under control and that no further problems would be occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And that was what you told Colonel Mrksic, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About me seeing Vukasinovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That was what you just told us?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't tell him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What was it you didn't tell him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What didn't I tell him? I told him what I was supposed to tell him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about what you have just shared with us, don't you think you should have told him that, too?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And after all, all the other officers were present. I told him about the situation I had personally encountered at Ovcara, but that was the extent of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, I'm asking you whether you, at the time, shared with Mr. Mrksic what you have just told us, that the prisoners of war were separated from the TO men. Did you share that with Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And my question to you is: Why?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We may as well have talked about this later on, outside the building. I'm not sure whether I told him or not. I don't wish to commit on this, because I'm just not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you personally saw to it that order was re-established, right, and the fact that the POWs were finally apart from the TO men, that a rope had been set up. This wasn't something that you could just afford to keep silent about, right, you must have told him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may as well have told him, but the important thing for me was to tell him, to brief him, on what exactly was going on at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Precisely. You told him what had happened. You told him what was going on, POWs had been attacked, you're leaving the hangar, you're on the way to the command. Some degree of order is now established because these people are now physically separated from the TO men, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could Colonel Mrksic have told you and other commanders perhaps no more than the following words: "Don't even tell me about that," meaning: Take any measures that you can with your units, the units at your disposal. If that proves out to be insufficient, I hereby authorise that you use units from the military company -- of the 1st Military Company and the armoured vehicles through the Chief of Staff of the operations group?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The way the question is framed is: "Could Colonel Mrksic have told," suggests a possibility. If my learned friend is actually saying that that is what Mrksic said to him, then it should be put to him in clear terms or what actually Mrksic did say, not the hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I heard what the witness said in answer to a question by my learned friend. I'm just checking whether the witness perhaps heard something else in addition to that. I will be clear enough in keeping with Rule 90(H) when the time comes, but this is in reference to something that Mr. Moore raised in examination-in-chief, and that's why I'm raising the matter now, whether perhaps the witness heard anything like that. The phrasing was therefore deliberate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I heard nothing like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vojnovic, on that day you had under your command units totalling more than 100 people, plus some armoured vehicles in the Jakubovac-Grabovo-Ovcara area, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was it not logical for you that you get reprimanded by the commander for not using everything that you had, since you came there and told him that the situation in the hangar was not fully under control?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not quite like that, Mr. Vasic. I did have the means, I did have the manpower, but there is something you seem to be refusing to understand. We had nothing with this particular assignment. It should have been done without us. It should have been done without our knowledge even. I just happened to be there, but all those units were not supposed to be used for anything like that. The fighting had stopped, there was no combat. What do you want me to say? Should I have used tanks against those people who were unarmed?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who is unarmed, Mr. Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When I suggested that you should have used tanks, I didn't mean that you should have used the tanks against the prisoners; should have used them against those threatening the safety of the command post and all those around?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was an officer from Operations Group South who was their commander and who had brought them there. It was his place to establish order and to keep them at bay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you see him exercise command there actually?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was the most senior officer there. Wasn't us who brought them there to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That wasn't you, but your war log reflects precisely what your assignment was, although you claim to have been unaware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were brought there; they didn't just come of their own accord. An officer was placed in charge of those people, and he was the responsible one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, would you agree with me if I told you this: Never prior to your testimony before the special court did you ever mention that your own chief of security, Dragi Vukosavljevic, came to the command post of OG South with you, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't remember that Dragi Vukosavljevic was with me. But I know Dragi to be a very good, very conscientious officer, and I lend my full credence to whatever it was that he stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I understand, you will take his word for it, but did you actually hear him say anything and what was it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean about the command -- the command post of OG South?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No. I mean Dragi Vukosavljevic, you telling him that he was at the OG South command post and you accepted this, but this obviously wasn't prior to 2003, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came to the OG South command --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, I'm asking you, you based this on something Dragi Vukosavljevic had said. You found out about this and you believe him; it's that simple.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about when, when did you find out what exactly it was that Dragi Vukosavljevic had said and where? To whom did he state this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the body or the court where he stated this, but I do believe this; this was something that Dragi said and I believe him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I do understand that you believe him, but did you hear this from the horse's mouth, as it were, or you read this on the internet, in one of the daily newspapers or magazines, or perhaps you were given a statement that he had made?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know if it was the internet or some report or other.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Knowing Dragi Vukosavljevic, you accepted his story in full, in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you don't remember the story yourself you have just told us, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The story when he came to Mitnica, but when the -- I mean OG South, but when or how, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement to the investigative judge of the special court, Judge Alimpic, did you tell him that Mrksic said that he had other duties and that he didn't order anything else in relation to the situation at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't say that to me. He said that to Dragi Vukosavljevic. To me he said, "Don't tell me anything about it," and he didn't do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So this part that I quoted is actually something that you heard from Dragi Vukosavljevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And that is in his statement -- actually, that is in the information that you had about his testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where I noticed that, but I did read about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one matter that does concern me is the way that a question has been framed. We have had to take time to check it. My learned friend has suggested, I think, that this witness has never mentioned about Dragi Vukosavljevic being with him at the meeting at the headquarters of Mrksic. We have had a look at the Novi Sad transcript, and that does not seem to accord with the way the question was put. I don't know if my learned friend is aware of that. I'm having to look at two documents, and it's not easy to follow. But if that's the case, then there has been an unintentional misleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I appreciate that. My learned friend is reminding me, and correcting me, but in my question I actually said that the witness before he gave statements before the special court never mentioned this. The transcript in Novi Sad that my learned friend, Mr. Moore, is talking about, is actually the transcript of the testimony of this witness before the special court. So I don't think that I was improper or incorrect when I put this question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, do we have the transcript in the folder that you submitted to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a statement to the investigative judge of the district court in Novi Sad in the folder, it's a statement from the 21st of November, 2003. So what I showed the witness were the statements he provided before 2003. This is what I was asking him about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: May I just suggest that you proceed with caution and take into account the observation by Mr. Moore. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, in the course of 2003 did you contact the other protagonists of the events at Ovcara who were members of the 80th Motorised Brigade? Did you see them, speak with them over the phone, meet them, speak with them before and after testifying before the organs to whom you gave your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really say with certainty whom I saw, whom I met, and who I talked to by phone, but I did follow the testimonies they gave, either at the district court, and I don't know where else. With some of them I did speak, that's correct. And one time I think that I saw Vezmarovic in Kragujevac; I went there. My daughter graduated at the law faculty there, so we went for her graduation, her final exam, and that's when I saw him. We didn't really talk about it. We didn't talk about it or -- and we didn't think that it would ever happen that we would be called as witnesses so much. Our part, we thought, was over, with the testimony at the Novi Sad district court, but unfortunately it was not. But, yes, and of course I also saw Dragi, but I don't know whether that was on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you meet in Kragujevac just like that? You didn't attend any court hearings, you just met?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- yeah, I went with my daughter, she was attending the law faculty. It wasn't my intention to go specially because of that. I went because of my daughter, in the same way that I spoke with you in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Of course. On that day when you met Mr. Vezmarovic and Mr. Vukosavljevic, you talked about the Ovcara events, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Dragi didn't want to talk about anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you meet any of those people earlier in the presence of General Aleksandar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never actually saw General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, perhaps a couple of times we shook hands. But I did hear that he talked with Captain Vezmarovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about Vukosavljevic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Vezmarovic didn't tell me that, and I don't know whether he talked to Vukosavljevic or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How did you find out that he talked to Vezmarovic then?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think it was written somewhere that Vasiljevic talked to Vezmarovic. I think it was immediately afterwards in 1992 or 1993. I don't know if that is true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: From what we've heard from you today, we can conclude that you actively followed all the Ovcara trials, including this trial here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a normal thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you do that just like other members of the 80th Brigade did in order to find a way to lessen the degree of your participation in what happened at Ovcara and to reconstruct the responsibility of the command that was responsible for all those failings?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was really interested to see how things were evolving because many things were not known to us. Many things that are very hard for me to understand, as well as for others, are things that I found out on television or in the newspapers, things that were published. And it's strange that I didn't know that, even though I was an officer of a unit there. That was the only reason why I followed the events there and here, and I learned much more than I knew while I was in Vukovar and after Vukovar. I can say that in 1993 and 1994 my knowledge was very, very slight of all the events there. All that I knew was something that concerned Ovcara. I didn't think that that was all that important and that nobody would call me because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And in that way, you augmented your testimony before the trials because you said that what you knew about the Ovcara events was very slight, very moderate, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was slight.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that yesterday, before this Trial Chamber you said that for the very first time that Colonel Mrksic told you something along the lines of, "What were you doing here?" Is that the first time that you mention that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. "What were you doing there? Why were you there?" I didn't really pay attention to that. I thought that it would be quite sufficient if I were to say what I saw there, how it was, and that everything would turn out differently; and now I see that that is not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So now you see that that is not so. What I asked you was whether this was the first time that you said that before the -- this Trial Chamber. In earlier hearings you never said that Mrksic said anything like that to you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mrksic did say that to me, but I never mentioned it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did Mrksic tell you that in the operations room during the briefings?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first thing he said, "Don't tell me about it," was in the operations room, and the other thing is, "What were you doing there," this was outside when we went in front of the building, when we were standing in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that Mrksic went to one side and you went to the opposite side when you left the operations room, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps after that I went to my command, as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that Mrksic did not leave with you, did not leave the brigade command together with you, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps we did not exit together, but we did talk together in front of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was anyone else around?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officers were passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I were tell you that my client asserts that he never said anything to that effect and it's not in accordance with your entry into the war diary of the 19th of November, 1991, at 1900 hours, what would you say to me?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing to say to you like that. I just told you what I heard and what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You assert that your superior officer said: "What were you doing there?"

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And you know that your unit was ordered - at least we heard that today - to take part in the security of the prisoners of war on the 19th of November, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was a completely different situation. Are you talking about the 20th of the -- and the Mitnica group? My unit did not receive an order to secure the prisoners from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We read the entries from your war diary of the 19th of November at 1800 hours. You say you don't know anything about it, but what I'm saying is: Does it not seem illogical to you that somebody is asking you: "What were you doing here," but an order was issued to your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No order was issued to my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You are stating that on the basis of not having looked at the documents of your units?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am stating that practically because my unit was never issued an order to that effect, either orally or in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have mentioned this matter before, that there never has been any reference to "order" on the 19th of November. There is no word that I have seen in either translation that refers to an order. There is an entry, but I don't see the word "order" anywhere. My learned friend keeps referring to it. Now, if there's an error in the translation, I accept that, but I have got two translations and "order" is not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend was present when we were reading that entry together with the witness, so I don't see what is in dispute here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that what is there does not necessarily have to be correct. One person was noting the entries down, and that's he wrote it down. I did say that I was asking for assistance to be sent to me from the brigade to help protect the prisoners. I think everything is clear in that respect, and not only is it clear, but this action actually happened. The officer came, he brought the men, reported to Major Vukasinovic, so that he could issue an assignment to him, asked him whether he needed assistance, and the other person said no, he didn't need assistance. The man again addressed him and said, if there is no assignment for him and no assistance is needed, then should he return to the unit, and he was told: There is no assignment for you. You can go and return to your unit. I don't know, perhaps something is written here, but this is how things actually happened, and this is something that was confirmed in practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... confused now, because I thought the point Mr. Moore was making was relating to the entry in the diary on page 10, the thing that we were discussing this morning and this question whether the translation of, "So it was arranged," as it appears in the English text, does not correspond to what is in the original. Maybe we should have this clarified. Maybe you should read from the original and have the interpreters interpret and see what it comes out in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the witness has been replying in relation to the 20th and not the 19th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we go on a break early, because then I could make the outline of my questions and I could find that relevant part? And then perhaps I can cut short my cross-examination. I think now we have been working for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... break and we hope that you can sort this out during the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, has the break enlightened you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Your Honour. First, I will try to meet my first promise, and that is the issue of the text initiated by my learned friend, Mr. Moore. I wanted to read it out in B/C/S, slowly. I believe that indeed the translation was erroneous. That is the entry for the 19th of November at 1800 hours from the war diary of the 80th Motorised Brigade. "During the morning the captured Ustashas were taken to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica. There is combat only in the hospital sector, and it is expected that the remaining portion of the ZNG and MUP forces will surrender (around 200). An order was issued to be prepared or to stand by regarding the organisation of securing those prisoners."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, is this what the text reads?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the text before me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't read the text that is before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you manage to read it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You don't have it on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I don't have it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need the entry for the 19th at 6.00 p.m. That is the last page, that is the one before last page of the war diary, Exhibit 375.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was it that you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I will read it out again, and perhaps you can follow. "In the morning the captured Ustashas were taken to the Sremska Mitrovica prison."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could the witness perhaps follow this, because he's not watching -- I believe he is, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: "There is combat only in the hospital sector, and the surrender of the remaining portion of the ZNG and MUP forces (around 200) there is expected. The order was issued to be prepared to organise the security of prisoners." Have I read it out correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would move on.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to clarify this somewhat. We were not familiar with any combat activities in the hospital sector. This was new information for us, we didn't participate there. As for the readiness mentioned to organise security for the prisoners, that is correct, but we haven't received any other task after this as to who was supposed to go where or do something.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, you told me you never heard of this assignment and that this was the first time you saw it here?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I heard of any combat around the hospital and that there were any prisoners at the hospital. This is what is stated here. And there is mention of being ready to be engaged, but we never received any such assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, you were not familiar with this order, and you stated that when I asked my question previously?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vojnovic, in your local command you had exclusive powers in the territory of Ovcara, Jakubovac, and Grabovo, and you could have undertaken any measures to prevent those events at Ovcara. And you had those powers at your disposal provided you assessed that either your units or the prisoners were in danger. Obviously you never made such an assessment as to the POWs?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My units were never endangered. The area where the prisoners were did not fall under my competence, it fell under the competence of the OG staff officers, and I have in mind particularly those who were at the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And you also didn't want to mention a particular name, because that was a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. At the time he was resubordinated to OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We've already discussed that topic, I believe. That is precisely what I said, that the Ovcara local commander on one hand, and you on the other hand as the local commander of Ovcara, Grabovo, and Jakubovac, that the two of you actually bear the responsibility for the tragedy that occurred in the hangar at Ovcara. That is why here you are trying to shift that responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Vasic. That was the area of responsibility of OG South. There were officers there, in particular the person who was there - not to mention his name - and the organ of OG South who was in the hangar itself. That area had been within my competence previously, but once those people were brought there and the officer arrived at the scene -- and by his appointment I held no authority over him, and I could issue in orders to him. Therefore, I couldn't have been responsible for that area of responsibility. I will clarify, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That is your explanation, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I have more. It is as if you were walking down the street and you tossed a bomb across the wall into my front yard, and then you say: It wasn't the blame of the person who threw that bomb, but the courtyard's owner's responsibility because he didn't have the time to throw the bomb back. That's the same situation here. Those officers came, and I could no longer have controlled the situation. For anyone to enter my AOR, they couldn't have done that without the permission of a superior officer or commander. And the person who has entered the area of responsibility, as you call it here, and if they wanted to abide by the rules, they had to have stopped by the aforementioned officer, and to inform him that he was under way with such and such group on such and such person's orders to stay there.
